description: Your hip is the biggest hinge in your body, and its tendons decide whether your legs swing like a pendulum or drag like luggage. Today you count relaxed leg swings, learn why the hip runs on cables instead of effort, and start waking the system up.

scenes.narration: Stand sideways next to a wall and rest one hand on it. Let the outside leg hang completely loose, like it belongs to somebody else. Now start it swinging, forward and back, the way a grandfather clock swings its pendulum. Do not kick. Do not force the height. Just let the leg swing and count how many full swings it makes in thirty seconds before the swing starts to shrink or your body starts helping. Then turn around and count the other leg. Two numbers again, and as always, the smaller one is the truth. At the end of this video I will tell you what that number reveals about the biggest cables in your body.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN STIFF AND FREE
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Twenty-eight relaxed swings in thirty seconds is where a stiff hip becomes a free one. Under twenty-two, your hip tendons are moving like cold rubber, and every stride you take costs extra muscle work. Over thirty-four, the leg swings almost for free, returned by the cables instead of dragged by effort. And watch the quality, not just the count. A swing that stays tall and smooth at second twenty-five is worth more than a frantic swing that falls apart at second ten.
scenes.sub: under 22: cold rubber hips - over 34: free-swinging

lines: the leg forward like a catapult.
beats.title: THE SLING

beats.text: MUSCLE STARTS IT, TENDON RETURNS IT

scenes.narration: Think about what a leg swing actually is. Your leg is a heavy pendulum, close to a sixth of your whole body, and something has to swing it forward thousands of times a day. Muscle starts the swing, but muscle is an expensive way to run a pendulum. So the hip uses cables. At the back of the swing, the hip flexor tendon at the front of your hip stretches like a sling being drawn. At the front of the swing, the big tendons behind the hip, the hamstring and glute attachments, stretch in turn. Each one stores energy at the end of the swing and hands it back at the start of the next. Walking and running are mostly this recycling system doing quiet work while the muscles make small corrections. When those tendons are trained, the pendulum swings tall and cheap. When they are neglected, the stretch shortens, the return weakens, and your muscles have to drag the leg through every stride like luggage. Your swing count is a grade of that recycling system. A high, smooth count means the slings are alive. A low, shrinking count means you have been paying muscle prices for a tendon job.

lines: Hip flexors held short all day
beats.title: SITTING SHORTENS THE SLING

scenes.narration: Now the uncomfortable part. The hip flexor tendon spends most of modern life held short. You sit in a chair, the hip bent, the sling slack and folded, for six, eight, ten hours a day. Tendons adapt to the length they live at. A cable that is never stretched slowly becomes a cable that cannot stretch, and the swing test exposes it immediately. Try this experiment on yourself: test your swings in the morning, then test again after a full day of sitting. Most guys lose several swings and feel the front of the hip pulling tight and dull. That is not damage. That is a tendon reporting its living conditions. The fix is the opposite input. Full, relaxed, repeated swings take the sling through its complete length under almost no load, which is exactly the signal that tells the tissue to stay long, slippery and elastic. Mobility work gets a bad name because it is usually sold as stretching. This is not stretching. This is tendon maintenance on the biggest hinge you own.

lines: The deep squat is the hip's
beats.title: SQUAT = FULL TRAVEL

beats.text: RANGE YOU USE IS RANGE YOU KEEP

scenes.narration: There is a second input the hip cables understand: deep positions. The deep squat, hips folded all the way down, is the position this joint was built to rest in, and it takes every hip tendon through its full travel at once. Cultures that still rest in a deep squat keep free-swinging hips into old age without ever doing a mobility routine. The joint is not lucky. It is simply used at full length, every day, for a lifetime. You do not need to live on the floor to borrow the effect. A few minutes a day in the deepest squat you can hold comfortably, plus your swings, covers both ends of the system: the sling stays long, and the deep tendons stay loaded. Range you use is range you keep. Range you abandon is range the body quietly sells off, one stiff morning at a time.

Here is the skinny advantage at the hip. The pendulum in this test is your own leg, and a lighter leg is a cheaper pendulum. Heavy guys swing more mass with the same size cables, so their swing fades sooner and their muscles pay more per stride. Your legs are light, which means your tendons can run the recycling system at a lower cost, for longer, with more practice before fatigue. Sprinting is nothing more than this test performed violently: the fastest men alive are not the ones who pull their legs forward hardest, but the ones whose hip slings return the leg fastest. Train the swing and you are training the cheapest speed you will ever own.

Now we wake the hinge up together. Hand on the wall, leg loose, swing. Thirty seconds, tall and smooth, then rest and change sides. Four rounds, two per leg. If your body starts helping, the set is over. Let the pendulum do it. Go.

Here is your week. Two minutes of relaxed swings, twice a day, plus three minutes in your deepest comfortable squat. That is the whole program, and it works because the hip responds to frequency, not punishment. Now the mistakes. Mistake one: kicking for height. The moment you force the swing higher with muscle, you stop testing the sling and start testing your effort. Loose beats forced, every time. Mistake two: letting your whole body rock and twist to keep the count alive. If the wall hand is doing gymnastics, the set is already over. Mistake three: holding your breath and bracing like a lifter. A pendulum cannot swing from a plank. Breathe out, stay tall, and let the leg hang like it is borrowed. Two extra smooth swings a week means the sling is lengthening. Slow, boring, and exactly how tendon changes.

scenes.label: RETEST - SAME WALL, SAME RULES
scenes.narration: So, your number, grading the smaller side as always. Under twenty-two: cold rubber hips, and every stride you take is costing you muscle money. Twenty-two to twenty-eight: the sling is waking up. Over twenty-eight: a free hinge, recycling energy the way it was designed to. Over thirty-four: your hips swing like a sprinter's warm-up, loose and tall. Put the smaller number in the comments. Just the swings. In thirty days we count again, same wall, same rules, and we see what frequency did.
scenes.sub: comment your smaller number - then beat it

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now we swing again, and the pendulum will report your attendance honestly. Subscribe so the retest finds you, and leave the smaller number in the comments where you cannot hide from it. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Why Your hip tendons Matter More Than Muscle (The hip tendon training Episode)
